author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
occasion: A festal encomium for the apostles Peter and Paul, celebrating their joint commemoration and praising their complementary roles in the Church.
argument: Hesychius opens by praising Peter with a chain of honorific images, then argues that adding Paul makes the apostolic pair an unbreachable wall, a double spring, and a harmony of opposites. He dwells on Paul's former violence as Saul and on Christ's gentle call, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?', in which Christ shows that he gave grace alongside the Law, that he fulfilled what the Law and prophets prefigured as types of himself, and that the prophets' oracles were about him. Paul's immediate faith is praised as a rebuke to heretics: Paul does not busy himself with questions but believes and worships without disputing. Christ's answer, 'I am Jesus the Nazarene whom you persecute,' reveals his identity as the eternal Son, David's son yet prior to David, maker of Abraham yet the one who crowned Isaac's altar, from Jacob yet the one Jacob saw on the ladder. The homily closes by contrasting Paul the former persecutor with Paul the evangelist, athlete, and intercessor, and ends with a doxology.

outline.move: The homily opens by praising Peter through a series of images, then says that with Paul added the pair becomes a double wall, spring, and harmony of opposites, and describes Paul's former violence as Saul.
Christ asks what harm he has done, shows that he added grace to the Law, that the shadows and types pointed to him as truth, and asks where Saul is aiming his weapons.

Paul answers 'Who are you, Lord?', and his immediate faith is praised as a rebuke to heretics; Christ replies 'I am Jesus the Nazarene whom you persecute' and unfolds his identity as eternal Son and creator.

Christ continues to show the futility of persecuting him, reveals he keeps Paul as bridegroom-leader of his bride, and notes that Paul will soon be persecuted for Christ's sake; the homily closes by contrasting Paul's former and present selves, cataloguing his sufferings, and ending with a doxology.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle Peter, praised as chief of the apostolic pair, fisherman, shepherd, and steward.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle Paul, formerly the persecutor Saul, converted by Christ on the road to Damascus.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: Jesus Christ, who speaks from heaven to call Saul and reveals himself as the eternal Son.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The psalmist David who sings and hymns Christ, contrasted with Saul who blasphemes and kicks.

voices.speaker: Christ
voices.how_marked: Christ's words are introduced with 'Σαούλ, Σαούλ, τί με διώκεις;' repeated as a refrain, but also include extended rhetorical questions and scriptural claims not introduced as direct quotation markers.

voices.speaker: Paul (as Saul)
voices.how_marked: Introduced with 'he answers and says'; his words are given in direct quotation, chiefly 'Who are you, Lord?'

key_terms.sense: One of the twelve apostles, here especially Peter and Paul as the apostolic pair.
A pair or team, here the apostolic pair of Peter and Paul.
A fishing net, used as an image for Peter's apostolic work and for the attempt to capture Christ.
Keeper of the keys, an image for Peter as steward of the treasury of divine gifts.
Repentance, the healing remedy prepared by Peter as a pharmacist.
The Law of Moses, which Christ fulfills and interprets.
Grace, which Christ adds to the Law as the good physician.
A type or figure in the Old Testament that points forward to Christ.
Radiance of God's glory, a title for Christ drawn from Hebrews.
Exact imprint of God's being, a title for Christ drawn from Hebrews.
A heretic, one who questions and disputes rather than believing as Paul did.
A proclaimer of the gospel, used of Paul after his conversion.
An athlete or contestant, used of Paul as one who endures sufferings for Christ.
To act as an ambassador or intercessor, used of Paul's continual prayer for believers.

scripture: The author cites the Septuagint and New Testament, using LXX book names and Psalm numbering. Modern citations should follow standard English Bible names and numbering, e.g. Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, Daniel, Jonah, Ezekiel, Hebrews, 2 Corinthians.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily is not stated in the text.
The precise occasion or liturgical setting is not specified beyond the joint commemoration of Peter and Paul.
